chapter.title: The Remote Account
chapter.sub: A login meant to live for three weeks has lived for ninety days. Somebody used it on Sunday.
chapter.status: **DRAFT** · scripted from the series plan · IDs provisional

items.text: SEASON 9 · EPISODE 1 · DRAFT · CASE-045  The Wyndmere, three months after opening · Maya, Solveig (head of security), Dario and Kit · Level L5 · Advanced support (formulas on request)  Maya’s first access review finds a login that was meant to live for three weeks. It’s been ninety days — and somebody used it on Sunday.  ⚑ RV-170: security owns access and any investigation. RV-171: governance only — no attack detail. RV-172: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: The Remote Account
items.stakes: An integrator's commissioning login is still live three months after handover — and someone used it at 03:12 on Sunday.
items.reward: Support that's named, approved and recorded — and a shared login that no longer works.

objectives.text: Decide what you do with what you found
Decide how the old door closes
Decide what stops the next one

items.rumor: The most dangerous account is the one everyone forgot.

items.alt: The Wyndmere's small security office: a wall of camera tiles, an incident screen reading ALL CLEAR; Kit points at a printed account list; Maya reads it.

bubbles.text: Eleven accounts on the control processors. I thought we had four.
And one of them logged in on Sunday at three in the morning.

items.caption: Three months after opening.

lines.text: Eleven accounts. I thought we had four.
So did everybody. That's why we look.

items.prompt: 10:10. ‘ext-support’ is still live, and it was used from outside at 03:12. What do you do?
items.risk: Lost evidence — or a door anyone could walk through.
timeout: The account stays live another week.

hints.text: Whose decision is an account — and what must survive until they make it?

options.label: Delete it now
options.result: Solveig, later: “And the evidence of who used it went with it — and the integrator's only way to fix a show.”
options.consequence: Destroys evidence and cuts support in one move.

options.label: Take the account list and the login record to Solveig; change nothing until she decides
options.result: Solveig exports the logs read-only, then asks Dario the questions with you.
options.consequence: Security owns access and the evidence; you bring the facts.

options.label: Log in as ext-support to see what it can reach
options.consequence: Makes you part of the log.

options.label: Message Dario: who's been using your login?
options.result: He asks his team in a group chat; the answer gets fuzzier.
options.consequence: The right question, asked by the wrong person, the wrong way.

items.title: Nine people, one password.
items.body: With Solveig in the room, Dario is straight with them. ext-support is his team's on-call login. Nine people know the password; two of them have left his firm. The 03:12 login was his current on-call technician fixing a stuck preset before a Sunday matinee — legitimate, and still untraceable to a person, unapproved and invisible to the venue.
items.label: Test: how much of the nine is gone — and was it an attack?

items.sub: Advanced · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Maya and Solveig beside a board. Nine people know the ext-support password. Two have left the integrator. It's been live ninety days since handover. Two of nine is twenty-two percent gone. Nine people for ninety days is eight hundred and ten person-days of exposure. And it's still the only way they can patch us. So we build the new door before we close the old one.

items.label: **Learn it now:** remote access — accounts, owners and offboarding.

items.label: **Sort it:** named, shared, service or orphaned?

items.alt: An account-review sheet: seven of the eleven accounts. maya.k and k.okafor named; booking-svc a service account; ext-support shared by nine people, t.hallan and demo orphaned, and techs shared with its password on the wall — the last four highlighted, with nobody as owner; ext-support's last login 03:12 from outside.
items.caption: Four accounts nobody owns.

items.title: The handover said ‘removed’.
items.body: Maya opens the handover checklist she helped write last season. Line 41: ‘Integrator remote access: removed.’ Ticked, initialled T.H. — the technician who left the integrator in the summer. No account list attached, nobody's second check. Fifty-nine other ticks look exactly the same.
items.label: Test: one false tick in sixty — and what would have made it true?

items.prompt: Wednesday. Solveig wants ext-support gone by Friday. How does the old door close?
unknown: Whether named sessions work with the integrator's tools
items.risk: A door anyone could walk through — or a show nobody can fix.
timeout: ext-support stays live over the weekend.

hints.text: What has to exist before the old login can go?

options.label: Security disables it tonight
options.result: Saturday a preset sticks and nobody can reach the processors until Monday.
options.consequence: Closes the old door before there's a new one.

options.label: Named accounts for Dario's team through a jump host security runs — each session approved and recorded — then security disables ext-support once a named session has worked
options.result: Thursday: six named logins, one test session recorded. Friday: ext-support refused.
options.consequence: The new door first, then the old one closes.

options.label: Change the ext-support password and send it to the seven who still work there
options.result: Seven people, one new password — the same problem with a new date on it.

options.label: Leave it, but watch the logs
options.result: Watching a shared login still can't tell you who.
options.consequence: A camera on an unlocked door.

items.title: The first hijacked demonstration
items.body: In June 1903 a physicist was about to demonstrate long-distance wireless telegraphy at the Royal Institution in London, as proof that the new system was private. Before it began, the receiver started tapping out Morse on its own — ‘Rats’, then a rude limerick about the inventor. A rival stage magician and wireless experimenter had tuned in from nearby to prove the opposite. The demonstration went ahead. So did the argument about who could get in.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #82 · AVERY'S LENS  Every account has an owner and an end date  An account nobody owns outlives the people who used it. Give each one a named owner, a reason and a date it ends — and check.  ‘ext-support’ was made for three weeks of commissioning. Ninety days later, nine people could still log in with it — two of them no longer worked for the integrator.

items.alt: The account-review sheet after the fix: the named and service accounts remain; ext-support, t.hallan, demo and techs greyed out and marked disabled by security; named access via the jump host, reviewed every quarter.
items.caption: Every account left has a name on it.

items.prompt: You could have just deleted it. Why bring it to me?

options.label: “Because it's your call, and deleting it would have deleted your evidence and the integrator's only way to fix a show.”
options.reply: Then you'll do reviews with me. Every quarter.

options.label: “I didn't want to get in trouble.”
options.reply: That's a reason. It isn't the reason.

options.label: “I wasn't sure how.”
options.reply: Good. People who are sure how are the ones I worry about.

items.title: ext-support · last login 03:12
items.body: The control processors' account list, exported read-only by security: eleven accounts. ext-support — created during commissioning — last login Sunday 03:12, from the integrator's VPN range.

items.prompt: Friday's review. What stops the next forgotten account?
known: ◉ Four orphaned or shared accounts found
unknown: What the signage and lighting systems hold
items.risk: The same finding next quarter, on a different system.

hints.text: Who would have noticed ext-support, and when?

options.label: A stronger password policy
options.result: The next forgotten account will have a strong password.

options.label: Every account gets a named owner, a reason and an end date; security runs a quarterly access review; the integrator's contract requires offboarding notice within a day; handover ticks need evidence attached and a second check
options.result: Solveig takes the review; Dario signs the clause; Nkechi adds ‘evidence attached’ to every handover template.
options.consequence: Owner, end date, review — and ticks that prove themselves.

options.label: Ban remote access
options.result: The integrator drives two hours for every stuck preset.

options.label: Make Maya the only admin
options.result: One person, one set of keys, one holiday away from nobody.

items.title: line 41 · ‘removed’ ✓
items.body: The S8 handover checklist, line 41: ‘Integrator remote access: removed.’ Ticked. Initials: T.H. — the technician who left the integrator in the summer. No evidence attached.

items.alt: The lobby during a Saturday matinee interval: every screen on the wall reads EVACUATE in red; the fire alarm panel beside it reads NORMAL; Tamsin, the duty manager, points; Maya stares.

bubbles.text: Forty seconds of that in the interval. No fire. My ushers held the stairs.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Every account needs a named owner, a reason and an end date. Measure exposure (% = part ÷ whole × 100; E = N × t) and take findings to whoever owns access — security. Build named, approved, recorded access before the old shared login is disabled, so nobody loses the ability to fix a show. Never use someone else’s credentials; never delete the evidence.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Which login in your world was made for a few weeks and is still there?
